Subject: Renewal planning — looking to right-size and limit renewal uplift

Hi Olga,

Thanks again for the meeting yesterday. BrightLeaf's usage profile has shifted heavily toward embeddings (search index refreshes) and a handful of inference-heavy batch jobs. We're evaluating the renewal and need a couple of things from Redwood to move forward with procurement:

- A recommended commit that reflects our new mix (we expect ~45% embeddings, 50% text gen, 5% reranking in token volume).
- A clear per-token discount ladder across commit tiers and a hard cap on renewal uplift (we need visibility if usage spikes vs. committed baseline).
- Any smoothing/true-up mechanics or short-term bridge credits you can offer during seasonal spikes.

Can you send an updated proposal and a simple spreadsheet model? Procurement also wants to know if you can lock a per-token ceiling so we don't see surprise effective increases at renewal.

Best,
Samir

Hi Samir — thanks for the clear summary. I've sketched three practical paths you can choose from and attached a short modeling workbook: Redwood_Commit_Options_v3.pdf (summary) and BrightLeaf_Renewal_Modeling.xlsx (spreadsheet). High level: 

Option A — Predictable Reserved: 12‑month committed spend, 20% per‑token discount from list at your current effective mix. Includes quarterly true-up window and a 15% seasonal bridge cushion for two quarters.

Option B — Elastic Commit: Lower baseline commit (6 months equivalent), stepped per-token discounts by threshold (3 slabs) and a soft uplift guard — we cap effective per-token increases to +12% vs. your current blended rate, with a usage-smoothing credit pool that auto-applies for transient spikes.

Option C — Pay-as-you-go with Anchor: No long-term commit, but we provide an anchor discount for the first 6 months and a one-time right-sizing credit if you hit a 6‑month smoothing target. This is less favorable on unit price but offers max operational flexibility.

A few clarifications and tradeoffs to call out: the per-token ladders are based on blended usage; shifting heavily toward generative tokens changes the effective unit economics — the spreadsheet includes a toggle to show that. The uplift guard (Option B) is the most explicit mechanism for limiting surprise increases at renewal — it sets an effective ceiling on per-token movement for the contract term.

Next steps: I propose we run the spreadsheet against your Q1–Q3 usage and confirm which option maps to your budget shape. Can we schedule a 30‑minute session later this week with procurement to walk the numbers?

Thanks,
Olga Petrov

Samir — quick add from pricing: we can codify the Option B formula this way (draft language for SOW):

"Effective per-token rate_t = base_rate * (1 - discount_tier) ;
If monthly usage > committed_monthly * 1.25, apply smoothing_credit = min((monthly_usage - committed_monthly) * smoothing_factor, cushion_pool);
Effective billed = max(effective per-token rate_t, base_rate * (1 - uplift_ceiling))"

Where uplift_ceiling is expressed as a percentage (e.g., 12%) and cushion_pool is the seasonal bridge pool (expressed in token-equivalent). I'll add the worked examples to the workbook and a simple audit CSV output so legal can see the monthly calculations.
